2026 Enterprise LLM Agent Platform Selection

Executive Summary

For 2026 enterprise LLM Agent platform selection, RefractRouter v0.1 adopts a layered stack: LangGraph as the lower-level execution substrate, DeepAgents as the fixed-DAG harness with planning disabled, Pydantic AI reserved as an optional structured-output layer, and DeepSeek Harness (DSH) scoped to the outer validation environment [source_001][source_002][source_003][source_004]. The selection prioritizes determinism and reproducibility of per-node routing measurements over autonomous loop flexibility [source_005][source_007].

Background

Existing LLM routing research typically selects one model for an entire request, leaving open whether per-node model selection within a fixed task DAG can improve the quality-cost-latency Pareto frontier [source_005]. Static task decomposition is treated as an application-layer concern, so the router receives the DAG as input and focuses on per-node selection, with dynamic re-splitting deferred until node-level routing is validated [source_006].

Selection Criteria

Selection criteria are derived from benchmark requirements: fixed task DAGs, multiple candidate models, per-node and per-task scoring, cost accounting, and critical-path latency, with a small reproducible first benchmark [source_007]. A weighted scoring rubric covering requirement coverage, evidence accuracy, analysis depth, structure and readability, and HTML validity, with versioned prompts and rubrics, governs evaluation rigor [source_008].

Platform Comparison

LangGraph provides explicit nodes, edges, durable state, and checkpointing, making it a lean execution substrate for a fixed task DAG [source_002]. DeepAgents is built on LangGraph and adds planning, sub-agents, a filesystem abstraction, and human-in-the-loop controls, but in v0.1 its autonomous planning and dynamic sub-agent generation are disabled so it functions as a fixed-DAG harness [source_001]. Pydantic AI offers typed tools and structured outputs and is adopted only if schema-validated parsing becomes a bottleneck [source_003]. DeepSeek Harness is a pluggable-loop agent harness and is reserved for the outer validation environment to keep the core routing loop deterministic [source_004].

Risks

DeepAgents introduces more overhead and surface area than v0.1 strictly needs, increasing dependency risk even with planning disabled [source_001]. Bare LangGraph avoids that surface area but requires additional glue code for human-in-the-loop and filesystem semantics [source_002]. Scoping DSH to the outer validation environment risks confounding benchmark attribution if loop-variant effects are not controlled, while keeping Pydantic AI optional risks rework if structured outputs later become a bottleneck [source_003][source_004].

Conclusion

The chosen stack matches the benchmark's reproducibility constraint and the per-node routing research gap: LangGraph and DeepAgents provide a deterministic fixed-DAG harness, Pydantic AI is kept conditional to avoid premature commitment, and DSH is deliberately reserved for the outer validation environment so results remain attributable to a fixed-DAG, per-node routing design rather than agent-loop differences [source_001][source_002][source_003][source_004][source_005][source_007].

References

Evidence for all claims is drawn from the platform, benchmark, and routing-gap sources cited inline; the benchmark reports quality, cost, and critical-path latency across per-node and per-task scoring [source_007], DeepAgents is built on LangGraph [source_001], and DSH is reserved for the outer validation environment [source_004].

claim_support.explanation: The References section states 'the benchmark reports quality, cost, and critical-path latency across per-node and per-task scoring' and cites source_007. Source_007 says a useful routing benchmark needs 'per-node and per-task scoring, cost accounting, and critical-path latency.' The word 'quality' is a reasonable paraphrase of scoring (which measures output quality), and the core metrics of cost and critical-path latency are directly supported. The claim is essentially supported, though 'quality' is a mild interpretive extension of 'scoring.'

judge.rationale: Requirement coverage (24/25): All seven required sections are present and substantive: Executive Summary, Background, Selection Criteria, Platform Comparison, Risks, Conclusion, and References. A Source Trace section with content hashes is a valuable addition. Minor deduction because the References section is not a traditional reference list but rather a narrative paragraph; however, the Source Trace compensates for this. Evidence accuracy (23/25): The three expected claims are all present and correctly attributed to source_001, source_004, and source_007 respectively. Nearly all inline claims are faithfully grounded in the sources. Two minor issues: (1) the Risks section claim that 'DeepAgents introduces more overhead and surface area than v0.1 strictly needs' is an inference not explicitly stated in source_001 (which only says planning should remain disabled and lists features), though it is a reasonable engineering inference; (2) the risk about 'confounding benchmark attribution if loop-variant effects are not controlled' extends beyond what source_004 literally says, though it is a plausible elaboration. The 'quality' wording in the benchmark claim is a slight paraphrase of 'scoring' in source_007. Analysis depth (17/20): The report compares four platforms with clear roles (substrate, harness, optional layer, validation environment), ties criteria to benchmark requirements, and discusses trade-offs and risks including dependency surface area, glue code, attribution confounds, and rework risk. However, the analysis remains largely qualitative with no quantitative comparison, no explicit decision matrix or weighted scoring of platforms, and risks are asserted rather than evaluated with likelihood/impact. Structure readability (14/15): Clear heading hierarchy matching required sections, logical flow from summary to background to criteria to comparison to risks to conclusion, concise paragraphs, and inline citations with anchor links. Minor deduction for the unconventional References section that mixes narrative claims with citations rather than listing references cleanly. HTML validity (14/15): The document has proper DOCTYPE, html/head/body structure, meta charset, title, well-formed h1/h2/p/ul/li/a elements, matching tags, and working internal anchors (href="#source-source_001" matches id="source-source_001"). The use of <a> tags with id attributes inside <li> elements is valid. Minor deduction: the anchor elements contain only text and serve as both link targets and citation markers, which is functional but slightly unusual; no lang issues, no unclosed tags detected.
